name: Yield Strategies in Smart Contracts
title: Yield Strategies in Smart Contracts
answer: Yield strategies in smart contracts are automated programs that move deposited capital across decentralised finance protocols to earn returns from lending, liquidity provision, staking, and arbitrage. The scope covers strategy design, vault contracts, aggregators, and the risk parameters that govern when funds enter or exit a position. These strategies are typically expressed as on-chain code with off-chain monitoring, and they operate without a human intermediary executing each trade. This page describes how such strategies are built and operated, not which yield a reader should pursue.

sections.body: Yield strategies in smart contracts are automated programs that move deposited capital across decentralised finance protocols to earn returns from lending, liquidity provision, staking, and arbitrage. The scope covers strategy design, vault contracts, aggregators, and the risk parameters that govern when funds enter or exit a position. These strategies are typically expressed as on-chain code with off-chain monitoring, and they operate without a human intermediary executing each trade. This page describes how such strategies are built and operated, not which yield a reader should pursue.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The strategies run on general-purpose blockchains that support smart contracts, most commonly Ethereum and compatible networks, using vault or strategy contracts that hold and deploy user deposits. They depend on price oracles for asset valuations, keeper bots or automation networks to trigger rebalancing and harvesting, and gas fee management to keep operations economical. Composability with lending markets, automated market makers, and staking contracts is the core infrastructure assumption, since a strategy is only as reliable as the protocols it calls.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by encoding rules that compare yields, utilisation rates, and incentive emissions across protocols, then moving funds when a threshold is met. Strategies often split capital between a base position and a more active position, rebalancing to capture higher returns or to reduce exposure to liquidation and impermanent loss. Off-chain simulations and backtests are used before deployment, while on-chain execution is handled by the contract logic and keeper calls. Monitoring focuses on slippage, collateral health, and changes in protocol rewards.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk centre on smart contract security, admin keys, upgradeability, and the provenance of the code and its audits. Users face protocol insolvency, oracle manipulation, impermanent loss, liquidation, and the possibility that a strategy contract has a bug or a malicious upgrade path. Governance votes may change fee structures, risk limits, or the set of protocols a strategy can use, and audit reports and bug bounty programmes are common forms of risk disclosure. Nothing on this page is legal, financial, or investment advice.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward more autonomous strategies that route capital across multiple chains, use formal verification for critical contract paths, and apply machine learning to tune parameters such as rebalance thresholds and collateral ratios. Institutional use is likely to bring custody, compliance, and reporting wrappers around the same underlying smart contract logic. The main open problems are reducing reliance on trusted keepers and oracles, and making strategy failure modes legible to non-specialist users.
